versions.notes:
- New Conversation game: play Blackjack against the house with up to six characters, from /blackjack or the games picker.
- Pick a character to deal and call each round in their own voice, or let the house deal silently.
- Hit, stand, double down, and split a pair once. Blackjack pays 3 to 2, and the dealer can hit or stand on soft 17.
- Set the starting chips, minimum bet, decks in the shoe, and an optional round limit.

- If someone is throwing a party or going to one, they won't make plans with you for those hours, even if you said you can't come. When you invite someone out, you can see the hours they have a party.
- If someone starts dating you knowing you already have a partner, they're okay with it. This also fixes the lives you're already playing.
- On a phone, you can drag the phone button with your finger.
- When a new season starts, people keep last season's outfit until the new one is ready.
- Fixes in the optional Adult Module.

- NPCs is a rule now, life by life: people who aren't in your cast, like a club's staff and its regulars. It's off by default in a new life; a life that already had them keeps it on. Off, they step aside with their pictures, nothing deleted.
- Once you're dating, you can stay the night at theirs, or have them stay at yours.
- No more getting stuck at the end of someone's party, after a lunch break that already went by, with a money request in the middle of an outing, or after reloading during a honeymoon night.
- In the optional Adult Module, the club's dancers and regulars are options that need NPCs.

- Cooking and food: a kitchen at home, twelve recipes, a Cooking skill, and dinner on a date at your place.
- A home of your own: Hillcrest on the hill, buying or a mortgage, furniture for each home, and people noticing where you live.
- People drop by, and you throw parties at home, lived room by room; friends throw theirs, and birthdays are parties now.
- Friends and family can live with you, as many as your home has rooms for.
- Anyone in the cast can be your family, partner, ex or rival from day one.
- Scenes do what's said: favours where they're told, money asked in your own words, outings that follow the talk, a memory for everyone there.
- Clearer Special Actions, work from home, half the practice for skills, and always a way on when the model can't answer.
- Many fixes, and more in the optional Adult Module.

- Contacts no longer freezes: opening it doesn't load your whole life again, and each part of someone's sheet is drawn on its own, so one that can't be shown is just missing and the rest is there.
- If a whole screen can't be shown, it says so, with a button to go back to the map, instead of leaving the game stuck.

- You can use your own pictures for what people wear each season or at work, and for you in any of your outfits: pick one and frame it yourself. Yours stays until you ask for a drawn one again.
- You can rename someone in Settings, and updating from their card brings a new name from the card too.
- When a model puts quotes in the wrong place or leaves part of a line out, the game still reads its reply, so turns in scenes aren't lost.
- The names on the clothes store's rack are sharp again. The phone's shop opens on its own inside a store, and going back returns you to the store with your cart.
- A fix in the optional Adult Module.

- People look like themselves in their pictures: their name, and whether they're a woman or a man, now go with every picture of them, so a character from a series looks like the one you know.
- You can choose how big pictures of one person are drawn, in Settings, right below the size of the other pictures.
- This season's new clothes are for who you play. A character who got dresses they'd never wear gets the season's clothes picked again.
- In the shops, only the things for sale move when you scroll. Eating from your backpack shows up on top of it. The clothes store shows the store behind the clothes again.
- The game finds Marinara however you run it, even from another device or on a secure connection.

- Models that think before they answer, like GLM or DeepSeek, no longer get cut off halfway: every call leaves them room to think, and one that still runs out gets a second try with more room.
- Reasoning has a new option, none, for models that can answer without thinking first.
- Pictures no longer flicker or load again while others are being painted, in Settings and on every other screen.
- Text on the phone, in the Guide and in What's New is sharp again.

- It looks more like a game: a new title screen, a welcome, a first-day card, the GUIDE (a searchable how-it-works app on your phone), a relationship chart in Contacts, and a redone profile.
- Everyone gets their own personality, read from their card, instead of twelve fixed types.
- Relationships go all the way: dating, moving in, engagement and weddings (with more than one partner if all agree), jealousy, open relationships and breakups, each in a scene.
- The town talks: people notice what you do, NEWS every Monday, and friends have opinions.
- Outings are one long scene; plans go on a calendar; birthdays.
- You start without a job: find one in JOBS, interview, get promoted.
- Money: BILLS, debt and eviction; HOMES to move. Five districts, and a motorbike or a car.
- Pictures of key moments, outfits by season, and manual or automatic pictures per life.
- Modules: optional extras you switch on for each life.

- First release, staging only: a modern life sim in its own Home tab.
- A town on a clock with places, opening hours, day and night, and four seasons of thirty days.
- A job, rent, needs and skills; a home with furniture, cooking and a closet; shops, a mall and online orders.
- A cast from your character cards: their weeks, archetypes and gift tastes read by the model, three bonds each, tier events, relationship steps and memories.
- Scenes told by a visual-novel narrator; sleep, knocking on doors and things to do together.
- Alpha: a save from before a change it depends on warns when opened.
- The Low magic layer's name and summary, and the magic items' Spell level filter, are translated in all 11 language packs.

- A Low magic layer, turned on when a game is created: magic is rare and feared. No spell above 5th level is offered, and no spell scroll above 5th level is found or sold. Every magic item still exists, but no shop sells one (the magic dealer and the scribe are gone, and temples and alchemists sell only mundane goods), treasure drops one about a fifth as often, and a town's fence is the one shady way to buy one. The Game Master keeps creatures of magic out of random encounters, may still build a fight around one on purpose, and, when the player gives no reason, decides at game creation why magic is rare in this world. Magic items' spell scrolls carry a Spell level filter. It needs Capability API 1.813.

- The whole SRD 5.1 in Game Mode: build a character from any SRD race, class, background and subclass, up to 20th level, and fight on screen by the SRD's rules against its 323 monsters, with its 325 spells, 966 magic items and every piece of equipment. It ships with 11 translations as language packs beside the English ruleset, and the Engine downloads only the one it is set to. It needs Capability API 1.812, whose numbers it now follows, upstream having taken 1.391 (the 5e minors move up one, to 1.392-1.812). A monk taken as a second or third class is proficient with shortswords, as the SRD's Multiclassing Proficiencies say.

- The first full release of 5e (SRD 5.1): the whole SRD 5.1 played in Game Mode, from character creation through tactical combat, in 12 languages. Its data is 0.451.0's; the version games pin keeps counting (452), so every existing game and install updates to it.

- No challenge 3 caster throws a 3rd-level spell that hurts everyone around it: a veteran battle priest casts Bestow Curse instead of Spirit Guardians, and a veteran pyromancer Magic Missile instead of Fireball (two veteran priests still wiped a 4th-level party in a Moderate fight, Spirit Guardians dealing over half the damage). The plain Arrow of Slaying names its 14 kinds and says a goblin takes Humanoid, a wyvern Dragon.
- Capability API numbers follow the Engine's renumbering after it merged upstream staging, where 1.379-1.390 are upstream's, so the 5e minors move up past them. Nothing plays differently.

- The 35 made-up casters (pyromancer, cryomancer, necromancer, enchanter, support, battle and nature priests) are as dangerous as their challenge rating: each rank's Armor Class, spell attack and save DC sit within 1 of its tier (novice and adept AC 13, +4, DC 12; veteran AC 15, +5, DC 13; master AC 16, +7, DC 15; legendary AC 18, +10, DC 18). A veteran battle priest cast Guiding Bolt at +8 and wiped a 4th-level party in a Moderate fight. The plain Arrow of Slaying says it is the family's name and to give an arrow of one kind, such as Arrow of Undead Slaying.

- Magic ammunition hits more often as well as harder: an Arrow, Crossbow Bolt, Sling Bullet or Blowgun Needle (+1, +2 or +3) adds its bonus to the attack roll as well as the damage (Capability API 1.812). It declares 1.812.
- The Light weapon property reads "Light (weapon)" on its chip and item tag, so each language can tell it from the Light cantrip: in Spanish it read "Luz" (illumination) beside the weapons.

- True Polymorph and Shapechange offer creatures only: a flying carpet, a dancing sword, an arcane hand, an illusory double or an animated object is no longer a form, nor what True Polymorph makes of an object. The creatures catalog marks what a spell, item or ability makes with a "Made by" filter.
- Spanish: the scimitar reads "Cimitarra" again, in its own name and the 22 other strings that name it (it read "Cimitaciónra").
- Polymorph and Animal Shapes leave out the SRD's ten swarms too, as Wild Shape does: a swarm is many beasts, not "a beast".
- Wild Shape no longer offers the SRD's ten swarms: a swarm is many beasts, not "the shape of a beast". The creatures catalog marks them with a Swarm filter.

- Every language's store-card description fits the Engine's 2,000-character cap, so the official catalog lists the SRD again: the German and French ones ran over (2,008 and 2,001). The sentence on starting equipment in your inventory is dropped from the description in every language, English included; the equipment itself is still offered.

- Translations ship as language packs, one download per language beside the ruleset file, and the Engine fetches only the language it is set to (Capability API 1.811): the ruleset file drops from 34 MB to 7 MB. The catalog lists each pack with its translated name and description for the store card.
- Each translation's package description says once, at its end, how to choose the ruleset, as the English one does: the earlier line, carried over from a draft, is gone.
- One long rest in 24 hours: "A character can't benefit from more than one long rest in a 24-hour period" (Capability API 1.810), counted on the game's clock from the start of the last one.
- Sheet layout 10: a sheet made before 0.438.0 has its cantrips marked prepared, so the GM's sheet summary lists them. The summary also names the character's features, fighting styles among them, and a warlock's invocations and pact boon.
- 81 more strings are translated, the Features tab among them.

- A carried weapon is drawn when it is used: the items block names weapons as drawn on use (Capability API 1.808), so a ranger's spare Longbow, a barbarian's javelins or a rogue's dagger can be attacked with without first being equipped, other drawn weapons put away. Only a character with Ritual Casting (a bard, cleric, druid or wizard, or a warlock with the Book of Ancient Secrets) casts rituals: the spells list names those features as what a ritual needs (Capability API 1.809). It declares 1.809.

- Translations for 11 languages (Arabic, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Brazilian Portuguese, Russian and Simplified Chinese) ship in the ruleset file: every name, label and rules text, plus the package name and description. The license attribution stays in English.

- Ritual spells can be cast as rituals, for no slot, outside a fight: the spells list names its Ritual column as the ritual mark (Capability API 1.807). Cantrips come onto the sheet prepared, since they are always ready, so the GM's sheet summary lists them. It declares 1.807.

- Attribution for release: the package's license names SRD 5.2.1 (the encounter budget table) beside SRD 5.1, with its CC BY 4.0 notice, and credits the Open5e srd-2014 data; it says the SRD material was adapted and reformatted, and that the package is not affiliated with or endorsed by Wizards of the Coast; the package description says it includes SRD 5.1 and 5.2.1 material under CC BY 4.0 and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Wizards of the Coast. The Engine's Capability API numbers from 1.385 up moved two places (upstream took 1.385 and 1.386), so every number the package names moved with them. It declares 1.806, so translations dropped in as locales/<language>.json ship with it.
- A long rest ends temporary hit points (Capability API 1.804): "they last until they're depleted or you finish a long rest".

- More "ww:" keywords, each one short thing: the world's shape on its "ww: world" entry (ww: city, ww: walls, ww: size large, ww: season winter); a place's hours and owner (ww: closed 22-6, ww: owner Mira); temperament and voice (ww: shy, ww: grumpy, ww: voice gruff); factions (ww: faction Thieves Guild, ww: member of Thieves Guild); and a creature's details, kept for later (ww: found in forest1, ww: night, ww: pack 4, ww: danger 2, ww: drops gold).
- Seasons: winter lays snow over the land.
- Four more ways to talk (gruff, formal, cheerful, sly), and a person can have their own.
- People made from lore get their details (who they are, manner, looks) from one model call, kept as their own card in the world. An owner a place names who isn't anyone yet becomes a new person.
- "ww: character Name" only ties to a card you chose for that world; cards you left out are never pulled in.

- "ww: character Mira Saxton": the entry is that person. A card of exactly that name is who it means and joins the world; with no such card (a "Mira Little" beside the card "Mira Saxton") a new person is made for that world. With no name after it, the entry's title is the name.
- "ww: monster Goblin", "ww: creature" and "ww: hostile" mark an entry as a creature. Nothing uses them yet: they are kept with the world (Journal → World lists them) for when the wilds have creatures.

- Lorebook keywords for Wanderworld now need the prefix "ww:" ("ww: tavern1", "ww:woman", "ww: lives in home3"), so a lorebook's ordinary trigger words ("town", "man", "enemy") never set anything by accident, and an entry's title alone links nothing. Lorebooks keyed the old way need the prefix added.
- New keywords: a day ("ww: work 10:15-18:45", "ww: home 22-7:15", "ww: eat 12-13 at tavern1"), a place's name ("ww: name The Gilded Stag" beside "ww: tavern1"), and "ww: character" to make a person of an entry with no card. Schedules keep quarter hours.

- New world can be written by the AI from nothing: "World lore: let the AI write this world and its places" writes a premise and named places with their own lore, kept in the world and active where you stand.
- "New people for the AI to invent": up to 12 people built around those places and your cast, with a description, personality, looks, home, work and relationships. They live in that world only (not Engine characters), talk and keep their days like anyone, and can't be cast in scenes.
- A lorebook entry about someone with no card can become a person in the world.
- The steps feed each other in order: lorebooks, the world and its places, new people, then your own characters fitted in among them. All of it shows in the review before the land is built.

- Dirt streets in a hamlet or village are paths now: their edges fade into the grass instead of ending in a hard line.
- A Large, Huge or Massive world left to the seed gets more places out in it (landmarks, and for Huge and Massive another farm and hamlet), so there is something to walk to. What you choose by hand stays as chosen.
- Fixed: your body picker in the bar didn't show the body the AI's setup gave your persona until the world was reopened.
- The AI's world setup has more room to answer (for models that think first), and the Journal's lore choices are worded as New world's.

- The AI's setup of a new world is shown before the land is built: everyone's body, home, work and relationships, the places the world will get, the names and the lore tied to them, with the map and world size. From there: build it, ask the AI again, or go back to the settings (the setup is kept).
- A model call that fails is tried once more; if it still fails, what did come through is kept, the review says what's missing, and "Ask the AI again" asks only for that. Building with a partial setup works, and Journal → World can finish it later.
- The loading screen now also waits for your own figure.

- New world can be set up by the AI, ready to play: it reads your characters' cards and persona (no lorebook needed) and any lorebooks you choose, and sets who's a man or a woman, how people know each other and you, where everyone lives and works, which lore belongs to which place, names for the places the lore names, and builds the places that takes. The loading screen says what it's doing until the world is ready. Journal → World can run it again. Lorebook keywords and setting things by hand work as before.

- Offered to Engine staging testers from Agents → Download Agents. The README has install steps, what each permission is for, known limits, and credits for the Quaternius CC0 packs the world is built from.

- Scenes you start in the world are planned by Wanderworld, so the Engine's scene dialog (with choices remembered from other chats) no longer comes up. Settings → AI: scene point of view, tense, and a prompt preset picked for every scene; Journal → World: scene instructions for that world. If planning fails, the Engine's own planner takes over.
- Up to five people hear what you say or do, and anyone you name ("/s Hey Ingrid!") is one of them if they're in earshot, with the nearest others.

- Moments: the "Around you" chat window takes what you say or do: plain text to everyone nearby, /s shouts, /w whispers, /p talks to your party, /a does something (open a chest, cast a spell). The narrator answers and whoever heard may reply. Reading the noticeboard, sitting by people and card choices are moments too. Commands are listed under the box; the window moves and resizes.
- Schedules: everyone follows a day (home, work, meals, visits, a seat), editable in Journal → People → Schedules, planned by the AI on request, and changed by what people agree to in moments.
- Illustrate: a window that paints the current moment from a prompt template you can edit, with a scrolling gallery (the newest 60): click to show, × to delete.

- A server part (needs an Engine restart after installing or updating): people answer in their own words, written by your model from their card, your persona, where you are, the time and weather, how they feel about you and the lore active there; set lines stand in if a call fails.
- Settings → AI: AI conversations on or off, the connections for conversations, scenes and pictures, how people talk, reply length, creativity, and the picture style (the Engine's style profiles).
- "Play it as a scene" on a scene card opens it as a roleplay scene in the Engine with everyone there; its recap comes back to Journal → Here.
- Journal → Here: "Picture this place" paints where you are through your image connection.
- The sound of rain while it rains (softer indoors), and no birdsong in it.

- Ponds: a landmark of its own, water in a hollow deep enough to swim in the middle and shallow at its sandy shore, ringed with reeds, ferns and mossy stones, with a bench looking over it. Comes with Landmarks in New world, or by the lore's pond1.

- Fix: a mill far along the river no longer stands in the water; it always steps straight across onto the town's bank.
- Rock on slopes blends in smoothly instead of painting whole triangles (sharp grey patches where level ground met a bank), and looks the same near and far.

- Chimney smoke darkens at night instead of glowing white against the dark sky; town walls are a darker, weathered stone.
- Every gate in a town's walls has a clear way out: a dirt track fading into the meadow where no road leaves, with no trees or bushes in the way.

- Hamlets, farms and landmarks keep all their ground inside the world, off the river, and clear of each other even in a crowded world: when their own side is full they find the nearest free spot elsewhere.
- A hamlet or farm goes on another side when there's no room for it beyond the river.
- Country roads wear away into the grass where they arrive instead of stopping square.

- Places out in the country keep clear of each other: a farm's fields no longer run into a hamlet, and two farms never overlap.
- A graveyard goes on a side of town the river doesn't cut off.
- Map names no longer overlap (each goes above or below its place, wherever there's room), and neighbouring regions have different names.
- The land goes on past the world's edge into the fog, with woods thinning out and the river running on, instead of ending in a drop to the sky.
